newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-B of E says no urgent need for rate rise.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-B of E says no urgent need for rate rise.

text.p: Bank of England Governor Eddie George said on Thursday there was no urgent need for a dramatic British interest rate rise despite the strong economic recovery, but he refused to rule out a rise before the general election.
"We don't see an urgent need for a dramatic step," he told the House of Commons Treasury Select Committee.
But when asked if this meant he expected no rate rise before the election he said, "I certainly wouldn't go that far".
A general election must be held by next May and financial markets are expecting at least another half point rate rise before then.
Most City economists expect George to call for higher interest rates when he meets Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke next week to discuss monetary policy.
Clarke agreed to George's request for a rate rise on October 30 and pushed up base rates by a quarter-point to 6.0 percent.

Asked by the Committee if he thought policymakers were now "ahead of the game" on monetary policy, George replied: "I think we were up with the game at the point when we raised interest rates in October."
He repeated the central bank's position that rates would have to go up again to enhance the chances of meeting the government's tough 2.5 percent inflation target.

"I would simply stand on the statement we made subsequently to that, which was that some further rate rise would be required at some point in order to give us a better than even chance of achieving the inflation target."
Recent inflation data have disappointed the authorities. Underlying inflation, which excludes mortgage interest payments, edged up to 3.3 percent in October, well above the target.
Economists are increasingly concerned that the lively consumer recovery may turn into a runaway boom, sending prices spiralling upwards.
Gavyn Davies, a member of the Treasury's panel of independent advisers, told the Treasury Committee last week that demand was growing at a "rapid and probably dangerous" rate.
But George said he did not expect to see a repetition of the 1980s economic boom. Britain was on the verge of an economic upswing but "not an 80s-type boom," he said.
The latest survey of the consumer sector showed retail volumes slowed in November.

The Confederation of British Industry, Britain's main employers organisation, said on Thursday that the number of firms reporting an increase in sales compared with last year dipped, despite expectations that it would rise.

"However, the upward trend in underlying sales remains encouragingly steady and consumers are expected to raise their spending in the run up to Christmas," said Alastair Eperon, chairman of the CBI's distributive trades survey.
The pound stumbled as dealers downgraded their rate expectations. It hit a session low of 2.5165 marks but recovered to 2.5301/11 marks in mid-afternoon trade.
"It was just becoming the case that interest rate expectations as priced in the market were losing touch with reality," said Adam Cole, UK economist at James Capel.

Short sterling futures, which reflect interest rate sentiment, bounced sharply. However, they still imply a small rise in official rates by the end of the year and a half point rise by the end of March.
This is in contrast to a poll conducted by Reuters last week which showed a majority of City economists expected the cost of borrowing to stay on hold until the end of the year.
The Financial Times index of 100 leading shares took comfort from sterling's fall and had gained 20.3 to stand at 4065.5 in mid-afternoon trade.
